title: Falsification of History
hook: After the result is known, the old uncertainty starts editing itself into confidence.
counterintuition: Memory can feel like evidence while quietly rewriting the past; protect the next decision by checking the record made before the outcome was known.
tryThisNow: Before revising one past decision, find one record from before the result and compare it with your current story.
keyTakeaway: Do not let today's outcome rewrite yesterday's uncertainty. Return to the record before judging the past.

breakdown.fastRead: A court team says it always knew the lunch calendar would fail, but the old price card shows a different story. Before the change, most people expected the schedule to work. After the result, memory edits doubt into foresight. That is history falsification. The past becomes cleaner than it was. The fix is to preserve records made before the outcome, then judge the decision against what was knowable then.
breakdown.deepRead:
A bad result makes the past look obvious. The donor letter failed, and now everyone remembers warning that the wording was too cold. The class filled late, and now everyone remembers knowing the deadline was wrong. The ferry sign confused passengers, and now everyone remembers predicting confusion from the start. Sometimes those memories are true. Often they have been polished by the outcome.

Falsification of history is not always a lie. It can be memory trying to make a coherent story. Once the ending is known, the mind edits the beginning. Doubt becomes certainty. Mixed views become a clear camp. The person who guessed both ways remembers the right guess. The team that was unsure remembers being wise.

The record is the antidote.

The correction is to keep pre-outcome evidence close. What did we write before we knew? What did the price card, trial binder, maintenance tag, or waiting-list sheet say at the time? What odds did we assign? What risks did we name? What alternative did we reject? If the record shows uncertainty, respect that uncertainty. If it shows clear warnings, respect those too.

This matters because rewritten history ruins learning. If every failure becomes 'we knew it,' no one improves the decision process. If every success becomes 'we were sure,' luck disappears from the review. Good judgment needs the messy past: the doubts, limits, blind spots, and information actually available at the time.
breakdown.fullRead:
The hospice donation letter raised less money than the spring campaign. By Monday, the story in the office is clear: the letter was too formal, the patient quote was buried, and everyone had sensed it. The trial binder says otherwise. In the draft meeting, three people liked the formal tone, two wanted a warmer quote, and nobody predicted a large drop. The failure is real. The new memory is too tidy.

History falsification begins when the present result reorganizes the past. People remember their earlier attitudes as more stable, more accurate, or more aligned with the outcome than they were. This is why postmortems often become theater. The group tells a cleaner story than the evidence permits, then learns from the story it just invented.

Gregory Markus's work on stability and change in political attitudes, later discussed in Kathryn Schulz's Being Wrong, points at the same pressure: people do not merely hold views and then recall them perfectly. They observe, recall, and explain through the lens of later belief. A past position can be pulled toward the present self. Memory becomes narrator, not archive.

What did you believe before the ending made belief easy?

A college add-drop deadline shows the pattern in miniature. After late complaints, advisers say they always knew the deadline was confusing. The maintenance tag on the registration system shows the old change request: shorten the reminder text because students ignored long emails. That was a reasonable guess. It was also wrong. The useful review asks why the guess failed, not whether everyone can now sound prophetic.

A ceramics shop sees the same thing after a defect discount. When customers buy the flawed bowls quickly, the owner says she knew the lower price was too low. The auction paddle from the pricing meeting shows a different debate: the team feared nobody would buy defects at all. The record does not embarrass them. It helps them learn the real lesson: demand was uncertain, and the next test needs smaller batches.

There is a limit. Records can be incomplete, defensive, or badly kept. A timestamp does not automatically tell the whole truth. People sometimes do give clear warnings that are ignored. The correction is not to worship documents. It is to compare memory with contemporaneous evidence before rewriting the story.

The best postmortem starts with artifacts. Put the old note, price card, email, binder, photo, calendar, or dashboard on the table. Ask what was known then, what was guessed, what was missed, and what only became obvious later. Once the past is allowed to be messy again, learning becomes possible. You stop punishing people for not knowing the ending and start improving how they reasoned before the ending arrived.

examples.title: The lunch calendar that everyone now knew would fail
examples.scenario: A price card from the courthouse cafe sits beside the municipal court lunch calendar at 1:15 p.m. in Albany. Norman, the court administrator, must decide whether to blame the scheduler after the lunch plan fails. He writes history falsification on the card, reads the prelaunch notes aloud, and changes the review from blame to a smaller demand test.
examples.whatToDo: Use the pre-outcome record to separate actual warnings from hindsight confidence.
examples.whyItMatters: The team cannot learn if a failed schedule becomes a story that everyone supposedly predicted.

examples.title: The donation letter with a tidy failure story
examples.scenario: "We all knew it was too formal," the fundraiser says while a trial binder lies open on the hospice conference table in Leeds. Gloria must decide whether to rewrite the annual appeal from memory or check the draft record first. She marks record risk on the binder, reads the split prelaunch votes, and changes the next test to compare warm and formal versions.
examples.whatToDo: Check the draft record before turning a failed appeal into a clean hindsight story.
examples.whyItMatters: The old disagreement is the useful data; the tidy memory hides it.

examples.title: The add-drop deadline everyone now remembers doubting
examples.scenario: The maintenance tag scratches Samuel's thumb at 8:30 a.m. as he pulls it from the college registration printer in Portland. As registrar for first-year courses, he must decide whether to accuse advisers of ignoring an obvious deadline problem. He circles memory risk on the tag, compares complaint dates with the old change request, and changes the review to test reminder length instead of rewriting blame.
examples.whatToDo: Compare current memory with the maintenance record created before complaints arrived.
examples.whyItMatters: A wrong guess can be improved only if it is remembered as a guess, not as ignored certainty.

examples.title: The defect price that looks obvious after sales
examples.scenario: You are holding an auction paddle from the 7 p.m. ceramics shop pricing meeting in Asheville while the sold-out defect shelf sits empty. Morris, the shop owner, must decide whether to say the low price was obviously foolish or review what the team believed before sales. He writes revision on the paddle, reads the old fear that defects would not sell, and changes the next batch to a small price ladder.
examples.whatToDo: Use the old uncertainty to design a better test instead of pretending the answer was obvious.
examples.whyItMatters: After success, memory can erase the fear that made the original price reasonable.

examples.title: The ferry sign that everyone now remembers hating
examples.scenario: It took Elliott two fog mornings at the Victoria ferry terminal's customer desk to notice how the passenger-sign story changed. As terminal operations manager, he sees the waiting-list sheet showing that staff had expected fewer questions, but after complaints everyone remembered the sign as obviously vague. He must decide whether to discipline the sign team. He writes narrative on the sheet, restores the prelaunch assumptions, and changes the next sign test to include confused passengers.
examples.whatToDo: Restore the original assumptions before deciding what the failed sign teaches.
examples.whyItMatters: A post-complaint narrative can make a reasonable but wrong assumption look negligent.

examples.title: The bakery leftovers that memory improves
examples.scenario: Did the bakery always know noon leftovers meant the croissants were too large? Harold pins a defect photo beside the Montreal bakery postmortem after three slow Fridays. The old prep sheet shows a different guess: rain, not size, was blamed at first. He writes falsification on the photo, compares weather and portion notes, and changes the next test to split batch size and daypart.
examples.whatToDo: Use old prep notes to keep the postmortem from inventing a cleaner cause.
examples.whyItMatters: A neat failure story can hide the actual uncertainty that needs testing.

reviewCards.front: A result makes the past feel obvious. What pre-outcome record should check memory?
reviewCards.back: Compare memory with notes, emails, probabilities, and risks recorded before the outcome. Later clarity often rewrites uncertainty.

reviewCards.front: Why is 'we knew it' dangerous after failure?
reviewCards.back: It can erase real uncertainty and turn a messy decision into a clean hindsight story, blocking learning.

reviewCards.front: What artifact should start a postmortem?
reviewCards.back: Use a pre-outcome artifact: old note, binder, price card, email, forecast, photo, or timestamp.

reviewCards.front: How can success falsify history too?
reviewCards.back: A good result can make mixed evidence feel like certainty, hiding luck and prelaunch doubts.

reviewCards.front: What should a decision note preserve?
reviewCards.back: Preserve reasons, odds, risks, rejected options, and the information available before the result was known.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use pre-outcome records to keep memory from rewriting the past after success or failure.

ifThenPlans.plan: If people say they knew the result, then I will put pre-outcome notes on the table before discussing blame.
If I make a meaningful choice, then I will record reasons, odds, and risks before the outcome arrives.
If a result succeeds, then I will check whether old notes show certainty or uncertainty.
If a result fails, then I will compare current memory with the original information set before changing policy.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one recent result you are explaining. Find one pre-outcome record and rewrite the lesson using only what was knowable then.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, write a decision note before the result, including what would change your mind later.

memorableLines.text: The past becomes cleaner than it was.
